subject: Climate & Environment
title: How Solar Panels Work
description: A 60-second lesson on How Solar Panels Work.

hook.text: A solar panel has no moving parts, no fuel, and no noise. It just sits in the sun and makes power.

buildup.text: Inside are layers of silicon — a semiconductor that reacts when photons hit it.

discovery.text: Photons knock electrons loose from silicon atoms, creating an electric current.

twist.text: This is called the photovoltaic effect. It was discovered in 1839 — not the 1970s.

climax.text: Modern panels convert about 20-25% of sunlight into electricity. That keeps improving.

punchline.text: Sunlight hits silicon. Electrons move. That's solar power.

quiz.question: What is the photovoltaic effect?
options: Light knocking electrons free to create current
Heat expanding metal to spin a turbine

details.summary: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic cells made of semiconductor materials, typically silicon. When photons strike the cell, they knock electrons free, creating an electric current. Modern panels convert roughly 20 to 25 percent of incoming sunlight into usable power.
details.whyItMatters: Solar is now the cheapest source of new electricity in most of the world. Understanding how panels work helps evaluate their potential and limitations for the energy transition.
takeaways: Photovoltaic cells convert photons into flowing electrons
Most commercial panels achieve 20 to 25 percent efficiency
Silicon is the dominant semiconductor material used

faq.question: Why can't solar panels convert all sunlight to electricity?
faq.answer: Only photons with enough energy can free electrons in silicon. Lower-energy infrared photons pass through, and excess energy from high-energy photons is lost as heat. These physical limits cap single-junction silicon efficiency around 29 percent.

faq.question: How long do solar panels last?
faq.answer: Most panels come with 25- to 30-year warranties and degrade at roughly 0.5 percent per year. Many panels installed in the 1990s still produce over 80 percent of their original output, and actual lifespans often exceed warranty periods.
